claude.sample_unit: patients across four external test cohorts (PCD mUC 94, PCD mRCC 58, Moreno 11, UNC-108 89)

links.outcome: Whether cohort-level applicability metric detects dataset shift relative to training data and tracks accuracy
links.effect: Applicability 74%, 76%, 71% with accuracy 69%, 83%, 86%; UNC-108 applicability 48% with accuracy 53%, flagged as shifted. Cosine distance alone was inconsistent (73% for UNC-108).
links.quote: In contrast, the UNC-108 cohort exhibited applicability below 60% and achieved a prediction accuracy of only 53%, indicating a substantial shift relative to the training data.

links.outcome: Prediction performance variation across independent cohorts/sites
links.effect: Accuracy 69%, 83%, 86% in three cohorts but 53% in UNC-108; precision 24% in UNC-108.
links.quote: LogitDA with our signature (ours) demonstrated stable performance in the PCD(mUC), PCD(mRCC), and Moreno cohorts, but only moderate performance in the UNC-108 cohort.

links.outcome: Performance on external test cohorts versus training data
links.effect: Performance degraded in external UNC-108 cohort (accuracy 53%) due to distributional shift; thresholds derived from only four cohorts and need further validation.
links.quote: A key limitation of transcriptomic predictors is their sensitivity to distributional shift, which can compromise reliability when applied to unseen cohorts.

links.outcome: Asymmetric score cutoffs minimizing false negatives across cohorts
links.quote: The associated false negative rates (FNRs; corresponding precisions) were 0% (41%) for PCD (mUC), 33% (40%) for PCD (mRCC), 25% (100%) for Moreno, and 27% (24%) for UNC-108 (see Table 1 for details).

unlisted_practices: Cohort-level applicability metric based on ORR-informed cosine distance as a distribution-shift safeguard
Asymmetric LogitDA score cutoffs with a not-applicable zone to prioritize minimizing false negatives

openai.sample_unit: patients in four independent test cohorts

links.effect: Accuracies were 0.69, 0.83, 0.86, and 0.53 across four independent cohorts.
links.quote: LogitDA achieved prediction accuracies of 0.69, 0.83, 0.86, and 0.53, with corresponding applicability estimates of 74%, 76%, 71%, and 48%, respectively, correctly identifying the UNC-108 cohort as one in which predictions warrant increased caution.

links.effect: Applicability estimates were 74%, 76%, 71%, and 48%, flagging UNC-108 where accuracy was 0.53.
links.quote: LogitDA achieved prediction accuracies of 0.69, 0.83, 0.86, and 0.53, with corresponding applicability estimates of 74%, 76%, 71%, and 48%, respectively, correctly identifying the UNC-108 cohort as one in which predictions warrant increased caution.

links.effect: Precision was 40% vs. 15%; PD-L1 found six true positives among 39 predicted positives.
links.quote: However, our approach substantially outperformed PD-L1 in precision (40% vs. 15%), as PD-L1 identified only six true positives among 39 predicted positives.

links.effect: FNRs (precisions) were 0% (41%), 33% (40%), 25% (100%), and 27% (24%) across four cohorts.
links.quote: The associated false negative rates (FNRs; corresponding precisions) were 0% (41%) for PCD (mUC), 33% (40%) for PCD (mRCC), 25% (100%) for Moreno, and 27% (24%) for UNC-108 (see Table 1 for details).

links.effect: Accuracy was 53% in the UNC-108 cohort with applicability below 60%, compared to 69%-86% in cohorts with applicability above 70%, reflecting marked degradation from distributional shift.
links.quote: In contrast, the UNC-108 cohort exhibited applicability below 60% and achieved a prediction accuracy of only 53%, indicating a substantial shift relative to the training data.

unlisted_practices: Cohort-level applicability scoring using response-rate-informed distance metrics to detect distributional shift

screen.practice: applicability check for distribution shift on new datasets
screen.reason: The study develops and empirically evaluates a decision-support GUI that includes an explicit diagnostic safeguard (an applicability metric/threshold) to detect distribution shifts and safeguard predictions across independent cohorts.
